message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  It is commonly expressed as the **Shannon number**, named after Claude Shannon, who first estimated it in 1950:

\[
N_{\text{positions}} \;\approx\; 10^{43}
\]

This figure is an estimate based on combinatorial arguments and is widely cited as a lower bound for the true count.  More recent analyses that take into account additional constraints (such as the fifty‑move rule, three‑fold repetition, and the exact rules for castling and en passant) suggest that the actual number of legal positions may be closer to

\[
N_{\text{positions}} \;\approx\; 10^{46}
\]

So, roughly speaking, there are on the order of **10 to the 43rd power** (or possibly up to **10 to the 46th power**) different legal arrangements of pieces on a chessboard that can occur during a game.

For comparison, the number of possible distinct games of chess (i.e., sequences of moves from start to finish) is even larger—estimated at about \(10^{120}\).
